verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains tabāraka, derived from barakah, as the stable establishment and subsistence of abundant good. Applied almost exclusively to God, it indicates that abundant good is firmly established in Him and thus emanates from Him to His creatures. Sending down the Furqān to His servant Muḥammad is one such benefit: it is a Book that distinguishes truth from falsehood, delivers people from error, and guides them.

Furqān, related to farq, may mean either that the Qur’an’s verses were revealed separately or that it discriminates truth from falsehood. The latter is confirmed by the Torah’s also being called Furqān although it was revealed at once; furqān is a stronger and more particular term than farq, used for the distinction of truth from falsehood. The Qur’an’s being a Furqān also proves its own truth: a false thing does not distinguish truth from falsehood, but confuses falsehood with truth in order to deceive.

Although ʿālamūn can include all created things, the context of warning confines al-ʿālamīn here to creatures charged with religious duty—humankind and the jinn, as far as is known. Thus, the claim that the verse establishes the Prophet’s mission to every being other than God is implausible, since it ignores this purpose of warning. The comprehensive plural, preceded by al-, includes all humans and jinn and implies that they have one God, contrary to the polytheistic notion that each community has its own god. Nadhīr means a warner, and indhār means warning or threatening; warning alone is mentioned because the verse’s tone is one of threat, though the call also includes glad tidings.

The verse consequently affirms that the Qur’an is from God; that Muḥammad is His messenger and servant, sent only as his Master’s obedient slave and not independently in charge of anything; and that he warns all nations through a Book separating truth from falsehood. Since a false messenger would not call to truth but depart from it, the Book and the servant who brings it establish the truth of his messengership; God further attests it through His miraculous Book. These points prepare the reply to the polytheists’ accusations that the Qur’an was fabricated with others’ help and that its messenger’s ordinary human life disqualified him. The view that Furqān means all revealed scriptures and “servant” all prophets cannot readily be drawn from the verse’s apparent wording.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan explains milk as possession or authority enabling one to manage and dispose of a thing, while mulk is the more particular authority of command and rule, such as a king’s dominion over subjects. The lām in lahu makes God’s mulk of the heavens and earth exclusive: nothing in them is independent of, or free from need of, His authority, direction, and management. He alone is their absolute Master and King.

Such absolute kingship negates God’s taking a son. A ruler adopts a child either because he cannot manage his affairs alone and needs assistance, or because his ownership is temporary and he needs a successor. Neither applies to God, whose power encompasses everything, whose ownership is eternal, and who is not subject to death or destruction. This refutes the polytheists and Christians. Likewise, an associate is needed only where one cannot command everything alone; since God’s command covers every being and every mode of its existence, He has no associate in the kingdom, refuting polytheism.

The statement that He created everything and determined it in a precise measure establishes that all direction and management return to Him. Creation (khalq) brings things into existence, while determination (taqdīr) gives them their form and measure. Created things and their properties are interconnected through preceding or accompanying means and causes; events in the visible world follow these created causes. Since there is no creator but God, no one else directs the universe. Creation entails measurement, and measurement entails tadbīr, the direction and regulation of affairs. Thus God is both King and Director, which together constitute His lordship (rabb).

The idolaters already acknowledged God’s universal kingdom, but supposed that He had delegated particular domains to lesser gods, each a king and lord within its own sphere. Mere affirmation of His kingdom would therefore not by itself refute their alleged partial lordships. The verse answers their underlying objection—that God might retain ultimate ownership while entrusting some affairs to associates—by joining His universal kingdom to His creation of everything and its inseparable measurement. Since creation and taqdīr together are tadbīr, the direction of every affair belongs to Him alone: no other kingdom or lordship exists, and it is inconceivable that He should delegate any affair to a creature.

Accordingly, the first part of the verse proves God’s unity in lordship and denies a child or partner through His absolute kingdom; its latter part explains that this kingdom rests on creation and precise determination, and therefore encompasses every rule and direction.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains that, since God is Creator and Designer of everything and possesses the kingdom of the heavens and earth, He alone must be served and worshiped. The polytheists instead worship idols that create nothing, are themselves created, and control nothing for themselves or others. The unexpressed pronoun “they,” referring to the polytheists, conveys humiliation and contempt.

The supposed gods are idols made by their worshipers through carving or other means. They are called gods only by name, without possessing any real divine quality: “They are naught but names which you have named; you and your fathers (53:23).” The indefinite negations stress the rebuke: people turn from the Creator of everything to things that have created absolutely nothing and are even created by their own worshipers and their imagination.

A being worshiped as a god must possess some good, since worship seeks the removal of harm or the attainment of benefit. Yet these idols cannot ward harm from, or bring benefit to, even themselves, much less to their worshipers; their worship is therefore insanity and error. The mention of “themselves” intensifies the reproach, and harm precedes profit because avoiding loss takes priority over acquiring gain.

Nor do the idols control death, so as to avert it from anyone; life, so as to give or take it as they choose; or resurrection, so as to raise people for requital. These are powers inseparable from the status of a god and lord, and the idols possess none of them.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan holds that “those who disbelieve” refers particularly to the Arab disbelievers, rather than to all polytheists. Their contemptuous reference to the Qur’an as “this” belittles it, while their charge is that it is distorted speech: Muḥammad’s own fabrication falsely ascribed to God. The “other people” who allegedly assisted him apparently were some People of the Book. Some narrations identify them as Torah-reading clients who later became Muslim and whom the Prophet visited.

The phrase that they “have done injustice and falsehood” most naturally means that they committed both; jāʾa and atā can mean “to do.” It may alternatively imply “they brought injustice,” but the reading that “injustice” describes the state in which they came is implausible. Although Majmaʿ al-bayān explains the brief reply by the prior challenge to produce the like of the Qur’an, Al-Mizan considers this phrase a general rejection rather than the complete answer to their accusations; the fuller reply follows in (25:6). Even taken independently, it rejects them by alluding to that unanswered challenge. Thus, their accusation that the Qur’an was forged with help from People of the Book is itself injustice and falsehood.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains that asāṭīr, though literally written reports, commonly denotes false or superstitious tales. Since the Prophet was unlettered, “he has got them written” cannot mean that he literally wrote them; it means that he had them written at his request, or asked for their writing. This is confirmed by their subsequently being read out to him.

Imlāʾ here means oral recital for a listener to retain, not dictation to a scribe. The disbelievers alleged that the tales had already been compiled in writing, then were repeatedly recited to him in portions, which he memorized, proclaimed to the people, and attributed to God. “Morning and evening” therefore means repeatedly and continuously, though some exegetes take it to mean privately at the beginning and end of the day. The whole verse continues the disbelievers’ speech and elaborates their preceding charge; Al-Mizan rejects the view that the latter part is instead God’s rhetorical response, since the verse’s tone and theme are uniform.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as commanding the Prophet to answer the accusation that the Qur’an was a fabricated collection of ancient myths. God’s knowledge of the secret—the hidden aspect of things—in heaven and earth indicates both that the Book contains realities inaccessible to ordinary human intellect and that God knows the accusers’ false claims.

Most exegetes understand “surely He is ever Forgiving, Merciful” to explain why God delays the punishment their denial deserves: the Qur’an is from God and contains hidden truths, yet He gives them respite through forgiveness and mercy. Al-Mizan rejects this. It would answer an unverifiable accusation by an equally unverifiable assertion, and Forgiving and Merciful more naturally indicate complete pardon than delayed punishment; names such as al-Ḥalīm, al-ʿAlīm, and al-Ḥakīm would better explain mere respite.

Rather, forgiveness and mercy explain why God sent the Book. God knows the inward secret of the disbelievers: their fiṭrah, which truly seeks perfection, felicity, and a good end in this world and the next. Though they wrongly locate happiness in worldly enjoyment, their innate state itself asks God for guidance. As Forgiving and Merciful, He answers that inward request by sending a Book that marks out the path of real felicity. If they accept it, His forgiveness and mercy embrace them; if they turn away, they are deprived of them.

This is a demonstrative proof of the prophetic call and of the Qur’an’s divine origin. A merely fabricated book would not consistently guide to true happiness and pure truth; it would sometimes direct people to what earns divine mercy and sometimes to what harms them and incurs divine anger. Thus the Qur’an is neither a forged lie nor ancient fable, but responds to what human fiṭrah secretly seeks.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that the disbelievers’ phrase “this Messenger” is scornful, since they did not believe in his mission. Their surprise that he ate food and went through the markets arose from their belief that material human beings, immersed in the world and its defilements, could not connect with the unseen. They regarded angels alone as near to God and capable of such connection, and worshiped them as intercessors.

They therefore considered ordinary human needs and earning a livelihood incompatible with a divine mission, which they thought could belong only to an angel. Their request that an angel be sent with the Prophet is a concession from this original position: if his human messengership is to be accepted, an angel must at least accompany him as a warner, connecting his message to the unseen.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan reads the demands for a treasure and then a garden as successive reductions of the disbelievers’ demand for an angel. Even if the Prophet were accepted as an unaided human messenger, they said, a heavenly treasure should free him from earning a livelihood in the markets; failing that, he should at least have a garden from which to live.

“The unjust” are the very people making these demands, and the explicit description underscores their transgression and defiance. Addressing believers, they call the Prophet “a man bewitched” in order to rebuke them and turn them from the true path. They mean that magicians had cast a spell on him, causing him to imagine that he was a messenger visited by an angel of revelation with a book and mission.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan says that al-amthāl here means the descriptions or likenesses the disbelievers applied to the Prophet. They described his eating and going to markets as proof that he was unfit for divine mission, since they imagined a messenger must transcend material attachments and ordinary means of livelihood; they also called him bewitched.

Such descriptions have led them far from the path, not merely into a slight deviation from which they could return. By calling God’s Book fables, describing His Messenger as bewitched, and persisting in mischief, defiance, and mockery of truth, they move ever farther away; in that condition there is no hope of their finding the way to guidance.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains that “better than this” refers at least to the demanded garden, and possibly to both the treasure and garden. The gardens with flowing rivers and the indefinite quṣūran, tall and strong palaces expressed with magnification, are far greater than what the disbelievers requested.

The shift from a direct response to “Blessed is He Who, if He will, shall give you” shows that the Meccan polytheists are unworthy of being addressed. They knew their demands were invalid, for the Prophet had only claimed to be a mortal like them who received revelation, not to possess independent supernatural authority. God therefore does not answer them directly, but tells His Messenger that the Lord who chose him and sent down the Furqān can, if He wills, grant him far more. The demand for an accompanying angel is left unanswered here because its invalidity is evident.

The gardens and palaces concern this world, since the verse occurs as a rebuttal in the present dispute: a promise confined to the hereafter would not answer their demand. Al-Mizan consequently rejects the interpretation that both are otherworldly, and still more the view that the gardens are worldly while the palaces are in the hereafter. The differing forms jaʿala and yajʿal occur in a conditional statement and do not establish different times; they are variation of expression and renewal of structure. God is the Knower.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan understands “Nay, they reject the Hour” as exposing the real cause of the polytheists’ rejection of the Prophet. Their criticism that he ate food and went through markets is only a surface excuse; their denial of resurrection and the hereafter makes prophethood pointless, for without reckoning and requital there is no place for religion and shariah.

It therefore rejects the view that the verse merely adds rejection of the Hour to a list of their false beliefs about God, the Book, and messengership. The surrounding passage remains concerned with their objections to the Messenger and its response, continuing through (25:20); the transition instead discloses the motive beneath those objections.

Saʿīr is a fiercely burning fire, prepared not only for the original audience but for every person who rejects the Hour. The use of the explicit description “him who rejects the Hour,” rather than a pronoun, establishes this universal rule and makes the threat direct and emphatic.
verses.12: Al-Mizan explains that taghayyuẓ is the manifestation of intense anger, sometimes with an audible sound, and that zafīr is the forceful inhalation and exhalation that expands the ribs. The verse portrays the Fire, when the disbelievers are presented before it on the Day of Retribution, as a ferocious lion roaring upon seeing its prey.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains thubūr as woe or destruction, and taqrīn as binding with chains and shackles; the alternative that it means being made companions of devils is not readily supported by the wording. The implied sense is that the condemned are cast into a confined place within the Fire while bound, where they cry out in overwhelming despair, “Woe! We are doomed!” (wā thubūrāh).
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains that crying wā thubūrāh is an appeal for rescue from distress. But the Day is solely a day of requital, when no beneficial action remains possible; thus calling for destruction, whether once or many times, will not help the disbelievers at all. The command not to call for one destruction does not primarily mean that their punishment lasts so long that it requires repeated cries, as some exegetes suggest; that interpretation is unlikely.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that “this” is the burning fire described previously. The Prophet is commanded to confront the disbelievers with the self-evident choice between it and jannat al-khuld: if they choose the Garden, they must abandon their former position; if they choose the Fire, they knowingly choose falsehood.

Khuld means perpetual continuance. The Garden itself is eternal, and its inhabitants are eternal and secure from perishing. It is the promised reward and final dwelling of the muttaqūn for their taqwā. They will have all they wish, but their wishes are not arbitrary: what they love is only what truly deserves to be desired, is good and felicitous, harms neither themselves nor others, and is pleasing to God. Being well-pleased with God and well-pleasing to Him, they will not desire sin, evil, vanity, anything that disturbs other inhabitants, the removal of decreed everlasting punishment, or ranks above those allotted to them.

The promise is binding upon God, having been decreed from the beginning of creation. Its description as masʾūlan may mean that the Godwary ask for its fulfilment through their state and capacity, explicitly through supplication, or through the angels’ supplication for them; all three may be true. Al-Ṭabrisī’s preferred grammatical analysis makes “That shall be a reward and a resort for them” a circumstantial clause describing the promised Garden, and “They shall have therein what they wish” one describing the Godwary, rather than treating both as independent explanatory statements.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan explains that “this” is the burning fire described previously. The Prophet is commanded to confront the disbelievers with the self-evident choice between it and jannat al-khuld: if they choose the Garden, they must abandon their former position; if they choose the Fire, they knowingly choose falsehood.

Khuld means perpetual continuance. The Garden itself is eternal, and its inhabitants are eternal and secure from perishing. It is the promised reward and final dwelling of the muttaqūn for their taqwā. They will have all they wish, but their wishes are not arbitrary: what they love is only what truly deserves to be desired, is good and felicitous, harms neither themselves nor others, and is pleasing to God. Being well-pleased with God and well-pleasing to Him, they will not desire sin, evil, vanity, anything that disturbs other inhabitants, the removal of decreed everlasting punishment, or ranks above those allotted to them.

The promise is binding upon God, having been decreed from the beginning of creation. Its description as masʾūlan may mean that the Godwary ask for its fulfilment through their state and capacity, explicitly through supplication, or through the angels’ supplication for them; all three may be true. Al-Ṭabrisī’s preferred grammatical analysis makes “That shall be a reward and a resort for them” a circumstantial clause describing the promised Garden, and “They shall have therein what they wish” one describing the Godwary, rather than treating both as independent explanatory statements.
verses.17: Al-Mizan explains that the plural pronouns refer to the disbelievers, and “these My servants” likewise means those disbelievers. If mā refers only to non-rational beings, “whatever they serve besides Allah” means their idols; if it can include rational beings, it also includes angels and human beings whom they worshiped. God will ask those objects of worship whether they led these servants astray or the servants themselves strayed from the path.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan explains that those whom the disbelievers worshiped first glorify God when asked whether they led His servants astray, for servitude requires glorifying Him whenever association with Him is mentioned. They deny that it ever befitted them to take guardians apart from Him; rather, the disbelievers themselves began worshiping them as guardians.

The worshiped beings attribute the worshipers’ error to the worshipers themselves. God had allowed them and their fathers worldly enjoyment as a trial, but, being a people in perdition—lost or corrupt—they immersed themselves in worldly desires and apparent means, forgot the reminder conveyed by the messengers, and thereby passed from monotheism into polytheism. “And they were a people in perdition” continues their answer and completes the temporal sense: they enjoyed themselves until they forsook the reminder and ended in perdition.

Al-Mizan rejects the claim that they were inherently doomed by God’s pre-eternal decree and that their error is attributed to them merely out of courtesy to God. This would make the preceding account of worldly enjoyment and forgetting the reminder pointless; it denies the efficacy of education and discipline, contradicts fiṭrah and empirical evidence, and conflicts with both ikhtiyār and jabr. It even conflicts with jabr because that doctrine makes the Necessary Being the sole cause, whereas this view assigns perdition to the essence of things.

God’s qaḍāʾ does not compel an act apart from the agent’s choice. Rather, His decree specifies the manner in which the act occurs, including its issuance through the person’s free will; decree thus confirms, rather than removes, volition. Nor can attributing evil to human agents be a courteous concealment of acts caused solely by God: if that were the truth, such attribution would be falsehood and libel, not adab. God is not glorified through falsehood or by dissociating His acts from Him.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that God addresses the polytheists after their objects of worship have dissociated themselves from them. Those beings will deny the polytheists’ claim that they are gods or guardians able to avert harm or aid their worshipers. Consequently, the polytheists will neither ward off their punishment through those beings nor find help through them.

The two terms distinguish independent protection, ṣarf, from assistance that is only part of a cause, naṣr. The reading transmitted by Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim has “you shall not be able,” while other reciters read “they shall not be able,” referring to the worshiped beings; the latter accords with the verse’s theme and means that those beings can neither avert punishment from their worshipers nor aid them.

“Whoever among you is unjust” states a universal law, not a punishment limited to polytheism, though polytheism is the immediate subject. Injustice includes every wrongdoing and disobedience. The abandonment of the polytheists by their gods demonstrates that nothing can obstruct or delay God’s binding decree: every unjust person will taste a great chastisement, and they therefore cannot escape it.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan presents this as God’s second answer to the objection that the Prophet eats food and goes through markets. All earlier messengers likewise had ordinary human qualities: they ate, went to markets, and were not given a garden for sustenance, a heavenly treasure, or an accompanying angel. The Prophet is no exception from whom unprecedented signs could rightly be demanded.

This reply addresses the objection as directed specifically against him. If it is generalized against all human messengers, its answer lies in the arguments concerning the rejection of the Hour and the Book sent by the Knower of secrets. Al-Mizan accordingly rejects the suggestions that the verse merely consoles the Prophet by earlier examples or answers the disbelievers’ defiance; their defiance was addressed by “See what likenesses do they apply to you…” (25:9).

The statement that God has made some people a trial for others explains why messengers share the ordinary life of those to whom they are sent rather than possessing overwhelming supernatural distinctions. The messengers test the people, separating skeptics who follow desire and cannot endure the bitterness of truth from truth-seekers who patiently obey God and follow His path. Patience includes patience in obedience, against disobedience, and through hardships and calamities. Although generally phrased, the trial here particularly concerns people’s testing through the messengers and their human qualities.

“Your Lord is ever Seeing” means that God knows what suits every matter, places all things properly, and governs through the most perfect order. In that order, people attain the perfection for which they are suited by the path of felicity or wretchedness; this requires trial and thus the removal of an outward distinction between messengers and other people. The shift to the third person, as in (25:10), also signals the disbelievers’ unworthiness of direct address.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains liqāʾ, the meeting with God, as humanity’s appearance before Him on the Day of Resurrection without the barriers of ignorance and heedlessness, when divine majesty is manifest: And they shall know that Allah is the evident Truth (24:25). Rajāʾ is expectation of a good thought likely to occur; consequently, those who do not hope for this meeting regard it as impossible and thereby reject the hereafter.

Their demand that angels descend upon them or that they see their Lord is therefore a challenge to the Messenger’s mission, not a request for its confirmation. They argue that if risālah—either an angel’s descent with revelation or God’s direct speech to a human—is possible for one human being, it should be possible for them as equally human beings. The demands are deliberately unconditional: they do not ask for an angel or vision to verify the Prophet, which confirms that they deny the very possibility of such a connection.

By saying “our Lord,” the polytheists mock the Prophet: although they treated their objects of worship as their lords and God as Lord of lords, they taunt him that, if God is also their Lord, He should choose them for direct vision and speech as He supposedly chose him. Their demand accords with their drift from worshipping unseen spiritual beings, such as angels and souls of stars, to visible idols representing them. God’s response, that they have sought unwarranted elevation and committed an immense revolt, condemns their arrogant self-assertion and shameless deviation from truth.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains ḥijran maḥjūran as a formula of protection: ḥijr is what is inaccessible through prohibition, and Arabs used the phrase when confronting someone they feared, asking for a prohibiting barrier between them. Khalīl reports its use by one fearing death during the sacred months, while Abū ʿUbaydah reports it as an Arab formula of protection in the Sanctuary or sacred months when bloodshed was feared.

The verse denies every kind of joy to the guilty when they see the angels. Although “the guilty” encompasses all sinners, its immediate concern is the polytheists who do not anticipate meeting God. The commentary prefers that “they shall say” refers to the polytheists, who appeal to the punishing angels for protection. Some instead make the angels say that good news, entry into Paradise, refuge from punishment, or perhaps return to the world is forbidden to them; but this does not fit the context as well.

The verse answers their demand for angels, not their demand to see God. They sought physical sight, which entails materiality and is impossible for the transcendent God; they neither sought nor, apparently, could grasp sight through the heart’s conviction. Their eventual vision of angels is certain, but it will bring punishment rather than benefit. Thus their demand is really a request to hasten punishment: We do not send the angels but with truth, and then they would not be respited (15:8).

Although exegetes commonly identify this day with the Day of Resurrection, Al-Mizan considers it more likely to be the day of death, when the polytheists first see and directly address angels after death and before Resurrection, in barzakh. The context demands this first unwelcome encounter, especially since they cry to the angels, “A forbidden barrier!” immediately upon meeting them. The verse and the following two therefore apparently describe barzakh: their encounter with angels, the annulment of their deeds, and the condition of the people of Paradise.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan notes that ʿamal is a voluntary deed of a living being, unlike fiʿl, which can also describe involuntary acts. Habāʾ is the fine dust visible in a sunbeam, and nathr means dispersal. God will turn every deed of the disbelievers into scattered dust, so that none of it benefits them after death, when one’s deeds determine the quality of one’s life.

The image expresses God’s wrath overruling and completely annulling the acts by which they sought happiness, leaving those acts without effect upon their eternal well-being. It resembles a victorious enemy entering an opponent’s house and destroying all its works and possessions. Although other verses indicate that disbelief and iniquity already forfeit their deeds in this world, there is no contradiction: the iḥbāṭ of those deeds is concealed from them here and will become manifest afterwards.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan identifies the dwellers of the garden with the muttaqūn mentioned in Say: Is this better or the abiding garden which those who guard (against evil) are promised? (25:15). Mustaqarr denotes an abiding-place, while maqīl is a place of midday rest, whether or not sleep occurs.

Khayr and aḥsan apparently do not function here as ordinary comparatives, much as “easier” and “better” do not necessarily imply a real shared quality in And it is easy (ahwan) to Him (30:27) and What is with Allah is better (khayr) than sport (62:11). Al-Mizan prefers to treat them as ṣifah mushabbahah: any comparative force arises from their roots and context, not merely their form. Since the polytheists treated their polytheism and wickedness as good, though these entail hell, they are told that the garden, the consequence of belief and Godwariness, is better than the end they chose. They must choose the garden rather than the Fire, and belief (īmān) rather than disbelief (kufr). Some exegetes instead take such comparative wording as mockery.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan takes yawma as the object of an implied command, “Remember the day when,” and identifies this as the Day of Resurrection, another occasion on which the disbelievers will see angels, as the next verse indicates. Other proposed grammatical analyses are not worth pursuing.

Tashaqqaqu means to split or burst open, and ghamām is cloud, so bil-ghamām may mean that heaven splits while covered by clouds, or that it splits through or from the clouds as they part. In either case, the apparent sense is that heaven, including its clouds, will split on Resurrection and its angelic inhabitants will descend for people to see, as in And the heaven shall cleave asunder, so that on that day it shall be frail. And the angels shall be on the sides thereof (69:16-17).

It is quite possible that this is metaphorical: the clouds are veils of ignorance, heaven is a portion of the unseen becoming manifest, and the angels come into view and descend into the human realm. Some exegetes relate it to They do not wait aught but that Allah should come to them in the shadows of the clouds along with the angels, and the matter has (already) been decided; and (all) matters are returned to Allah (2:210), taking the clouds as splitting heaven open. The choice of tashaqquq rather than a milder term for opening conveys terror, and the indefinite tanzīlān magnifies the angels’ descent.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan holds that on the Day of Resurrection absolute and unconditional kingdom will manifest as the exclusive right of the most Merciful. The apparent causal means and connections of this world will vanish, revealing that every rule, affair, and sovereignty has always been in God’s hand and that no force or cause acts independently. God’s kingdom does not begin on that day; rather, its reality becomes evident when the means that seemed powerful in other realms lose their apparent authority.

The day is hard for disbelievers because they relied on transient worldly means and severed themselves from the true Cause and possessor of all kingdom. Having cut themselves off from everlasting life and bliss, they will have no refuge. Grammatically, al-mulk is the subject and al-ḥaqq its predicate, whose definiteness indicates exclusivity, while yawmaʾidh marks when this truth is manifested. Al-Mizan rejects alternative grammatical readings that make kingdom mean ownership of the day, attach “on that day” to an omitted attribute, take it as “the Day of God,” or make yawmaʾidh the predicate and al-ḥaqq an attribute.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains biting one’s hands as the customary expression of intense remorse. The unjust will regret having failed in their obligations and wish that they had taken some way—indeed, any way—with the Messenger.

“The unjust” is generic, encompassing everyone who does not follow a messenger’s guidance, and “the Messenger” is likewise generic; at the time of revelation, however, they particularly applied to the unjust of this nation and to Muḥammad. The verse thus depicts their overwhelming regret: any path with the Messenger would have been better than their chosen end.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan takes fulān, “so-and-so,” as an indefinite reference to a male person, here the companion whom the unjust person befriended, consulted, listened to, and wrongly followed. It rejects the view that fulān specifically means Satan, since the context does not support limiting the word in that way.

The wording marks an escalation of desperation. In the preceding verse, the sinner cries yā without naming anyone, as though seeking any possible rescuer. Here he calls upon his own wayl—“O woe is me!”—showing that he now recognizes that nothing can release him from punishment except death and destruction.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains the reminder (dhikr) broadly as all the messengers’ teachings, though it may specifically mean their scriptures and, for Muḥammad, the Qur’an. The statement that Satan fails to aid man may be God’s comment or the unjust person’s remorseful addition.

Khudhlān is the abandonment by one expected to help. Satan promises help to those who cling to worldly instruments and forsake their Lord, but abandons them when God’s dominance severs those apparent means, partly at death and completely on the Day of Resurrection. Thus he says, after urging disbelief, I am surely quit of you (59:16), and: I cannot be your aider (now) nor can you be my aiders; surely I disbelieved in your associating me with Allah before (14:22).

The last three verses clearly indicate that error principally arises through attachment to people of base desires and to Satan’s crew.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan identifies “the Messenger” as Muḥammad, since the verse concerns the Qur’an. Calling him a messenger affirms his mission against those who disparaged it and his Book, while mahjūran, from hajr, means treated as abandoned or forsaken.

The commentary considers the statement to be the Messenger’s complaint to his Lord on the Day of Resurrection, linked to “the unjust one shall bite…” (25:27). Its past tense expresses the certainty of the future event. “My people” may mean all Arabs, but more likely the Prophet’s entire ummah, including its disbelievers and wrongdoers.

Alternative readings make the conjunction connect back to (25:21) or merely introduce a new statement, rendering the intervening verses parenthetical; Al-Mizan finds this unlikely in light of the passage’s flow. It consequently understands the people as those who criticized the Prophet’s message and derided his Book. It also rejects the weak derivation of mahjūr from hujr, “delirium,” rather than abandonment.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as God’s consolation to the Prophet: sinners have been enemies of every prophet, as part of God’s continuing way with prophets and their nations, so their hostility should neither grieve nor burden him.

God’s making sinners enemies is retributive. In punishment for their disobedience, He seals their hearts; they then oppose truth and hate its caller, the Prophet. Their enmity is therefore attributed to God in the sense that it follows from His requital of their own wrongdoing and choice.

“Your Lord” is sufficient as Guide because He guides all who deserve and are prepared for guidance; the denial of these sinners does not make others’ guidance dependent upon them. He is sufficient as Helper because He will aid the Prophet and the religion with which He sent him, even if the sinners withhold their support. The verse both comforts the Prophet and declares God, His Messenger, and His religion independent of sinners; calling God “your Lord” personally invokes His sustaining Lordship (rubūbiyyah).
verses.32:
Al-Mizan identifies the speakers as the Arab polytheists who rejected the Qur’an and had earlier called it a forgery. Their question, “Why has not the Qur’an been sent down to him all at once?”, criticizes its mode of revelation. Inzāl denotes a sudden descent, whereas tanzīl denotes a gradual one. Thus, the objection need not mean that they demanded a written book like the Torah, Gospel, or Psalms. The Torah’s reception as writing on tablets was an immediate act, while the Qur’an was received through the Trustworthy Spirit (al-rūḥ al-amīn), like speech heard from a speaker, which necessarily unfolds word by word. The polytheists’ demand was more fittingly that the angel recite the whole Qur’an to the Prophet on one occasion, rather than chapter by chapter and verse by verse. They did not themselves believe in the divine revelation of the earlier scriptures, so their objection cannot naturally rest on their supposed belief in the scriptures’ sudden written revelation.

Their underlying claim was that a genuinely divine religion should come as a complete, ordered whole, setting out its beliefs, laws, obligatory and recommended practices. They treated the Qur’an’s revelation amid changing events as evidence that Muḥammad was inventing speeches, calling them verses and attributing them falsely to God.

Al-Mizan explains kadhālika as referring to an implied “We have sent it”: God sent the Qur’an gradually and in differentiated series, not all at once, in order to strengthen the Prophet’s heart. Tathbīt is gradual establishment, and the Qur’anic heart is the rational soul characterized by understanding and cognition. Tartīl means bringing things one after another. The alternative reading that makes kadhālika part of the disbelievers’ question is deemed very implausible.

The gradual revelation strengthens the heart because instruction becomes rooted, transformative knowledge when it is applied in the real circumstances that call for it, rather than merely stored as an overall theoretical understanding. This is especially so for teachings concerning fiṭrah, whose receptivity is heightened by felt need. The Qur’an conveys Islam’s individual and social practices and laws, which rest on moral virtues; these rest on fundamental beliefs, which ultimately return to tawḥīd. Conversely, tawḥīd unfolds into the full system of belief, ethics, and practical law. Such teaching is best imparted progressively as events require explanation of belief, virtue, and law, accompanied by admonition through accounts of former peoples and the fate of transgressors, the haughty, and the extravagant. This is the sense of gradual revelation in (17:106).

Gradual instruction might seem liable to make earlier lessons fade before later ones arrive. “And We have arranged it well in order” answers this: although the revelation is differentiated, its parts are sent consecutively and in logical connection, so that their links and effects are preserved and the purpose of teaching is not defeated.

The Qur’an is also a book of argument and clarification, addressing followers’ and opponents’ doubts, correcting misunderstandings about earlier religions and scriptures, and disputing erroneous beliefs about God, angels, jinn, and human saints. Since disbelievers repeatedly raised doubts against the Prophet and tempted believers, revelation came progressively to answer problems as they arose. This is the further aspect introduced by the following verse.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains bi-mathal as a description or attributed account, and tafsīran as an especially clear exposition. Whenever the disbelievers bring an erroneous description of the Prophet or others, God brings the truth or the best clarification: a wholly false claim is replaced by truth, while a truth distorted from its proper setting is restored to its proper place.

Verse (25:33) therefore supplies, alongside the strengthening of the Prophet’s heart in (25:32), a second reason for gradual revelation: it answers the people’s false descriptions and distorted accounts as they arise. Verse (25:34) complements this response. Al-Mizan rejects exegetical attempts to detach the clauses of (25:32), treat (25:33) merely as an explanation of how the Prophet’s heart is strengthened or only of his attributes, and regard (25:34) as unrelated. The three verses form one answer to the disbelievers’ disrespectful objection to the Qur’an’s gradual revelation.

The commentary also rejects proposed additional reasons for gradual revelation as inadequate. The claim that gradual revelation was necessary because the Prophet was unschooled is not decisive: faithful Companions could have written a complete revelation, and God’s promises to preserve the Prophet from forgetting and to guard the Reminder apply whether it is sent gradually or at once. Nor does the Qur’an’s miraculous eloquence require gradual production, since a complete book can also possess proper order and eloquence. Abrogation does not mean cancelling a former law, but the expiry of its period of applicability, and both laws could be revealed together with the first law’s endpoint stated in advance. Questions may be answered before they are asked, events may be reproved before occurring, and past or future events may be reported beforehand. None of these considerations prevents a one-time revelation; some reduce in any case to strengthening the heart. The Qur’an’s stated answer is therefore complete.

Al-Mizan reads “Those who shall be gathered upon their faces to hell” as an indirect reference to the same disbelievers, who apparently inferred from their criticism that the Prophet was in an evil plight and had strayed. God avoids explicitly repeating this evil description of prophethood and instead reverses their charge: those who truly are in an evil plight and far from the path are the mockers, not the Prophet. “Worse” and “farther away” need not be comparative; they may echo and rebut the form of the opponents’ allegation, though a comparative sense is possible in a rebuking tone. The indirect wording is both more expressive and threatening, because it indicates their evil end and punishment.

These are deniers of the hereafter, whose objections are captious and whom God leaves to stray. Their being gathered on their faces toward hell manifests their worldly error: the one moving on his face cannot see ahead, and this is the utmost straying. Majmaʿ al-bayān reports that the disbelievers had called the Prophet and believers the worst of God’s creatures; other exegetes connect the verse with the dwellers of the garden in (25:24). Al-Mizan holds that its connection lies instead in the implication supplied by its theme and context.

The apparent meaning of being gathered on their faces is retained: they move while flat on their faces. Interpretations that mean merely being dragged, moving upside down, humiliation, an idiom for not knowing one’s destination, or a figurative attachment to worldly ornaments are problematic. If upside down were meant, the wording would be “upon their heads”; metaphor is unwarranted where the literal meaning is possible; and “to hell” does not fit ignorance of one’s destination. The final figurative view may, however, refer to the lingering effects of worldly attachment. In light of verses concerning tajassum al-aʿmāl, their punishment represents their lifelong attachment and orientation toward the world, becoming their sole occupation in the hereafter.

verses.35: Al-Mizan states that Moses’ being given a Book, appointed a messenger, and aided by his brother Aaron confirms the truth of Prophet Muḥammad’s messengership and the Qur’an’s revelation in the face of the disbelievers’ denial. It also prepares for the account of Pharaoh’s clan being punished and exterminated.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains tadmīr as an unusual, harsh destruction. The āyāt rejected by Pharaoh’s people are God’s signs in the horizons and souls, pointing to His unity. Abū al-Suʿūd’s view that they are specifically Moses’ nine miracles is acceptable only if evidence establishes that specification. On that reading, the verse calls them rejecters although Moses and Aaron were ordered to go before the signs were shown, because God speaks of them afterward and thereby explains why they were destroyed: the two prophets showed them the signs, they persistently rejected them, and God destroyed them.

Together with the preceding verse, this account threatens those mocking the Prophet’s Book and message by comparing his mission with Moses’, who received a Book and was sent with Aaron to Pharaoh’s people; their rejection brought utter destruction. Moses’ Book is mentioned before the mission and Pharaoh’s drowning, although the Torah came afterward, because the narrative selects and orders what serves this purpose: the granting of a Book, Moses’ messengership, and the destruction of deniers. The view that these verses instead relate to “and sufficient is your Lord as a Guide and a Helper” (25:31) is unlikely.
verses.37: Al-Mizan takes “the people of Noah” as governed by an omitted verb implied by “We drowned them.” Although they rejected Noah in particular, this is equivalent to rejecting all messengers because the messengers share one message of truth; as idolaters, they denied prophethood and messengership altogether. Their drowning made them a sign for the descendants who remained after them, while a painful punishment awaits the unjust.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan connects “ʿĀd and Thamūd and the dwellers of the Rass” to the destruction of Noah’s people: God likewise destroyed ʿĀd, the people of Hūd; Thamūd, the people of Ṣāliḥ; the dwellers of the Rass; and many generations between these peoples from Noah’s time onward. Qarn means people living in one era, and can also mean the era itself.

Majmaʿ al-bayān defines rass as an “unfenced well.” One reported view identifies its dwellers as a people who settled by a well after Thamūd, rejected God’s messenger, and were exterminated. Another identifies al-Rass as a river where they lived, a view supported by some Shia narrations.
verses.39: Al-Mizan explains that “to everyone” means each of the peoples already mentioned. God gave them examples—that is, admonition, advice, and warning—but, because of their denial and defiance, utterly destroyed them. Tatbīr means crumbling, fragmenting, or grinding to pieces.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan identifies the town as that of the people of Lot, upon whom God sent a rain of stones of clay. The rhetorical rebuke asks whether the polytheists, who repeatedly passed it on the route from Hijaz to the Levant, did not see it.

“They did not hope to be raised again” may mean either that they did not fear resurrection at all or that they wholly dismissed its possibility. Their denial of the hereafter is the root of their rejection of God’s Book and Messenger, their failure to heed admonitions, and their refusal to learn from the destruction of former deniers. Thus they turn a deaf ear to the religious call, and wisdom and admonition do not settle in their hearts.
verses.41: Al-Mizan explains that the plural pronouns refer to the disbelievers previously mentioned. Huzuwan, though a verbal noun synonymous with istihzāʾ, here has an objective force: when they see the Prophet, they treat him only as one to be mocked. Their question, “Is this he whom Allah has raised to be a messenger?”, is itself the form their ridicule took.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains that in is shortened from inna, and that iḍlāl with ʿan means turning away. The disbelievers say that the Prophet nearly turned them away from their gods and would have done so had they not persisted in worshipping them; whether the conditional’s consequence is omitted or its order is reversed, the meaning is the same.

Their seeing the punishment is a divine warning: then they will know with certainty that they, not the Prophet, were the ones farthest astray from the path.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan defines hawā as an inclination of the soul uncontrolled by reason. Taking one’s low desire as a god means obeying material desire rather than God, since ṭāʿah of something amounts to its ʿibādah. The rhetorical question denies that the Prophet is a protector or master of such a disbeliever who can guide him after God has led him astray and cut off his means of guidance.

The commentary holds that “takes his god to be his low desire” has its natural grammatical order: “his god” is the first object and “his low desire” the second. Idolaters do not reject the need for an object of obedience; they know that a god should be obeyed, but wrongly make desire that object, replacing the Truth with it. This accords with the context of their polytheism and aversion from obeying God. The reverse parsing, proposed by other exegetes to express surprise or exclusivity, is therefore implausible.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan takes am here as a transition rather than an alternative conjunction, and ḥusbān as supposition. Hearing and understanding are the two routes to guidance: one either recognizes and follows truth through independent reason, or listens to one able to discern it and sincerely advise. The verse asks whether most of these people can do either, such that one might hope for their guidance.

They are compared to cattle because they neither properly hear nor understand the truth, though they hear sounds. Indeed, they stray further: animals do not deliberately prefer harm to benefit, and lack the human faculties that lead to guidance, whereas these people possess those faculties but abandon their direction by following desire. The comparison does not deny either animals’ knowledge of their Lord or the disbelievers’ knowledge of God altogether; it concerns the specifically human rational faculty. Al-Mizan finds no proof for reducing the verse to a merely apparent comparison.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan reads verses (25:45) onward as illustrations of divine guidance, not primarily arguments for tawḥīd. God sends the Messenger to rescue people from error; some whom He wills are guided, while those ruled by low desire neither hear nor understand and cannot be guided except by God. The extension and removal of shade, the alternation of night and day, and rain reviving dead land all show a consistent divine way of dispelling deprivation. The two seas and human kinship further illustrate how distinction is maintained amid shared proximity and unity, like the distinction between believers and disbelievers.

In (25:45), the extended shade is specifically the shadow after midday, gradually lengthening west to east until sunset, though God could have made it stationary. It analogizes error spreading over those whom God has not willed to guide, while the prophets’ call removes it as the sun removes shade. The shift to “your Lord” addresses the Prophet in particular to deny that he has power over their guidance; the disbelievers are not addressed because they follow desire and neither hear nor understand.

The sun is an indication of shade because changes in sunlight disclose the shade’s existence and its expansion or contraction; in general, altered possession or loss is what makes people perceive things. The return to the first-person plural expresses divine grandeur. The subsequent verses alternate between the third-person mode of “your Lord” and the majestic plural, in parallel with this verse.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains that God takes the shade to Himself as the rising sun gradually removes it until it vanishes. Calling this removal a gentle taking displays God’s absolute power and indicates that what disappears after existing is not annihilated but returns to God.

The commentary maintains that the shade in the preceding verse is the growing shadow after midday, an interpretation it considers unprecedented but consistent with the context. It rejects interpretations referring to the interval from dawn to sunrise, nighttime shadows, the shadow cast by a solid object, or the primordial shadow of heaven upon the earth; it judges the last especially weak.
verses.47: Al-Mizan explains that night is libāsan because its darkness covers people like clothing. Sleep is subātan, a cessation of activity, while day is nushūran, a time for people to spread out from their homes in search of sustenance. Thus God covers them with night, interrupts their movement through darkness and sleep, then brings daylight for renewed work and endeavor, paralleling His extension, indication, and gentle removal of shade.
verses.48: Al-Mizan explains bushran as an elided form of bushur, the plural of bushūr, meaning bearers of good news: God sends winds announcing His mercy, namely rain. Al-samāʾ means what is above, the atmosphere over the earth. Ṭahūran intensifies the rainwater’s purity: it is pure itself and purifies other things by removing dirt, filth, and defilement.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan takes baldah here in the general sense of land or place, explaining the masculine mayt despite baldah’s feminine form. A dead land has no vegetation, and giving it life means causing plants to grow; anāsī is the plural of insān.

God sends pure water upon land overcome by death, reviving its vegetation and giving drink to its cattle and many people. This is another instance of the preceding analogy of shade: deprivation is removed through God’s life-giving act.
verses.50: Al-Mizan takes “it” to mean water. God turns rain about among communities, directing it from one place to another at intervals, so that neither continuous rain nor complete absence of rain destroys a people and each place receives its fitting share. This distribution is meant to make them mindful and thankful, yet most people respond only with denial and ingratitude toward God’s blessings.
verses.51: Al-Mizan reports the exegetical interpretation that God could have raised a warner and messenger in every town, but instead raised Muḥammad as warner and messenger for all towns because of his great standing before God. This is supported by the following verse and fits the passage’s connection. Alternatively, the verse may simply affirm God’s power to raise a messenger in every town while indicating that His choice of Muḥammad rests on wisdom and consideration.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan explains that the opening fāʾ draws a conclusion from the preceding verse, and that “with it” refers to the Qur’an. Mujāhadah and jihād mean exerting one’s utmost ability against an enemy; striving with the Qur’an means reciting it to the disbelievers, explaining its realities, and leaving them no excuse.

The Prophet must not follow the disbelievers, but remove the veils of ignorance and heedlessness by clarifying truth and completing the proof through the Qur’an. His mission is like the sun removing shade, day succeeding night, and rain reviving dead land. Since he has been sent as a warner to all towns, he must exert his fullest effort in this Qur’anic call.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan explains maraja as mixing or blending, but the barrier in the verse clarifies that the two seas are placed beside one another rather than mixed together. ʿAdhbun furāt is sweet, potable water, while milḥun ujāj is intensely salty, bitter water. A barzakh separates them, and ḥijran maḥjūran means that each is prohibited from mixing with the other.

Joined to the signs in (25:48), this is an analogy for the religious message: believers and disbelievers may live in the same land and mingle, yet remain distinct from one another.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan explains ṣihr, on the narration from al-Khalīl, as in-laws or a wife’s relatives, contrasted with nasab as relatives on the man’s side. The verse may also be read as making human beings possessors of both kinds of relationship. Its water may mean sperm, a kind of water, or water in the absolute sense from which all living things are created.

The verse thus describes God’s creation of the human being from sperm and division into possessors of nasab and ṣihr, namely man and woman. It illustrates plurality and dispersal within unity: as humanity is one yet differentiated through its relationships, so people living together remain distinct in belief and disbelief through the messengers’ call, which lifts the veil of error. “Your Lord is Powerful” addresses the Prophet as in (25:45), since guidance belongs exclusively to God.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan explains ẓahīr as muẓāhir, one who assists. The polytheists serve idols that neither benefit their worshippers nor harm them if they cease serving them; in doing so, the disbelievers are Satan’s assistants against their Lord.

The idols’ inability to harm does not mean idolatry is harmless. They themselves have no power to act, but serving them necessarily leads to eternal punishment and wretchedness.
verses.56:
Al-Mizan holds that the Prophet was sent only to give glad tidings and warnings, not to control people’s affairs. He is therefore not accountable when they oppose their Lord and aid His enemy: they cannot render God helpless but only plot against themselves. The verse reiterates the meaning of “Will you then be a protector over him?” (25:43).

The commentary rejects the view that the verse merely consoles the Prophet by distinguishing believers, for whom he brings good news, from disbelievers, for whom he warns. That reading does not accord with the context.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan takes “it” to mean the Qur’an, whose recitation conveys God’s message and fulfils the Prophet’s mission. The exception, “except for him who wishes to take a way to his Lord,” is grammatically disconnected in form but effectively connected: it means the act of taking a way to God by whoever wishes to do so. The people’s acceptance of the call of truth is therefore the only reward the Prophet seeks, not wealth, rank, or any other payment; this demonstrates his sincerity.

The qualification “who wishes” preserves their freedom. The Prophet’s task is only to convey glad tidings and warnings, without compulsion, vengeance, or guardianship over them; belief or disbelief is their choice, while judgment belongs to God, on whom the Prophet must rely.

The commentary rejects the majority view that the exception directs anyone wishing to compensate the Prophet to give charity in God’s way, since neither wording nor context supports it. It regards the interpretation that makes belief and obedience his reward as substantially similar to its own, but objectionable for requiring an omitted muḍāf. It also rejects the view that he seeks God’s reward for others’ belief, because reward follows actual action, whereas the verse speaks of wishing.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan explains that, having limited the Prophet’s task to conveying the truth and left people free to choose, God commands him to take God as guardian over their affairs. God will judge and treat them as He wills, for He is guardian over them and all things. He is called “the Ever-living Who dies not” because nothing escapes or is missed by One who never dies, and He is thus fit to be relied upon.

To glorify Him with praise is to declare Him free from weakness, ignorance, and every imperfection, while affirming His excellence. If He grants bounties as istidrāj or hastens punishment, neither results from weakness or ignorance: each follows His wisdom and the recipients’ worth and capacity. God alone manages His servants, knows their sins, and judges them without assistance.

Together with (25:59), the verse establishes the life, knowledge, and kingdom required of a wakīl: “the Ever-living Who dies not” affirms life, His awareness of sins affirms knowledge, and His creation and rule affirm sovereign authority.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse completes the grounds for relying on “the Ever-living Who dies not” (25:58). A wakīl requires life, knowledge, and authority to manage: the preceding verse establishes life and knowledge, while God’s creation of the heavens, earth, and all between them, and His establishment on the Throne, establish His authority.

The commentary reads al-Raḥmān as the predicate of an omitted subject—God is the Beneficent—and fa-isʾal as a consequential command. In fa-isʾal bihi khabīran, bihi connects “ask” to God with emphasis, while khabīran describes Him: ask God, the Aware One. God, established on the Throne, sustains creation and directs affairs by mercy and grace; all things begin from Him and return to Him. One should therefore ask Him about the reality of the matter, because what He reports is exact truth.

Al-Mizan rejects the many alternative grammatical readings that make al-Raḥmān independent, attach it differently within the sentence, take bihi as “about,” or make khabīr someone other than God—whether Gabriel, Muḥammad, scriptural scholars, or any knowledgeable person—because they do not accord with the verses’ theme and context.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as another instance of the disbelievers’ mistreatment of the Messenger and their arrogant refusal to prostrate to God. Al-Raḥmān is the Beneficent just described in the preceding verse, and the Prophet is the one who calls them to prostrate, although their response reveals that their opposition is truly against God.

Their use of “what” rather than “who” in asking about the Beneficent feigns total ignorance of God’s reality and manifests pride. Repeating “what” in “Shall we make obeisance to what you bid us?” is disrespectful, while calling the Prophet’s summons an amr is mocking derision. The command to prostrate only increases their aversion.

The commentary rejects the report-based interpretation that “it adds to their aversion” refers to the Prophet’s own act of sujūd. The text refers instead to his command that they prostrate, and an external event cannot determine the meaning without textual indication.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan identifies the sirāj as the sun and takes burūj to mean either the solar and lunar mansions or the stars. Their name, literally strongholds, signifies their function as guards and missiles against devils.

The commentary rejects the common reading that the verse primarily argues for a single director of the ordered heavens and earth. In its context, after the disbelievers’ defiance of the Beneficent and mockery of His Messenger, the verse instead shows God’s dominance and needlessness: they cannot defeat Him or leave His kingdom. They are barred from approaching the divine precinct and its teachings, whereas it is illuminated for God’s special servants by the guidance brought through Muḥammad.

God’s praise of Himself as Blessed includes His guarded constellations, which fend off devils with flames, and the luminous sun and shining moon. These physical realities illustrate the true illumination of the human world by messengership, which grants insight to God’s servants, and the prevention of devilish agents from rising toward Him. This contextual interpretation remains within the apparent meaning and is not taʾwīl.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan explains khilfah as mutual replacement: night and day each succeed the other and can take its place for one who wishes to remember God or give thanks. “Remembrance” is mindfulness of the innate knowledge of God to which fiṭrah points, and thus amounts to belief in His unity, names, and attributes. “Thankfulness” is speech or action appreciating His blessings, and thus amounts to His ʿibādah and righteous deeds.

The alternation of night and day manifests God’s domination and grace, allowing one who missed belief in one period to make it up in the other, and one who missed worship or a righteous deed at night or by day to perform it in the other. Although some exegetes limit remembrance to obligatory prayers and thankfulness to recommended prayers, Al-Mizan regards this only as one application, not the verse’s full meaning.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan contrasts the believers with those who arrogantly derided the name al-Raḥmān: God calls the believers His servants and attributes them to Himself by that very name. Their “walking on the earth in humbleness” (hawnan) most plausibly describes their whole manner of living and associating with people. As servants of God, they are inwardly humble before their Lord and humble toward people, neither proud before God nor seeking undue ascendancy over others. Yet they are not subservient to God’s enemies in pursuit of their favor or illusory power. Hawn may alternatively mean lenience and moderation (rifq, līn), denoting freedom from pompous and pretentious conduct.

The “fools” (al-jāhilūn) are identified by their quality of jahl: they address believers with speech arising from imprudence and ignorance, which is burdensome and unpleasant. The believers answer with “peace,” speech free from vanity and sin, rather than answering foolishness with foolishness. The verse thus depicts their conduct among people during the day; their nighttime conduct follows in the next verse.
verses.64: Al-Mizan explains that baytūtah means passing the night, whether asleep or awake. The believers spend the night before their Lord, alternating between prostration and standing in worship; the daily prayer (ṣalāh) is a clear instance. The verse may specifically refer to keeping the night vigil through the recommended night prayer (ṣalāt al-layl).
verses.65: Al-Mizan explains gharāman as an affliction that strikes a person, remains with him, and does not depart. The believers therefore pray that their Lord turn from them the enduring punishment of hell.
verses.66: Al-Mizan explains that “it” refers to hell. Mustaqarr and muqām denote, respectively, a place of settlement or residence and a place of stay; hell is evil in both respects.
verses.67: Al-Mizan defines infāq as spending or using money to fulfill one’s own needs or those of others. Isrāf is spending beyond the proper limit, while qatr, iqtār, and taqtīr mean spending too little. Qawām means the middle, balanced, and just course. Thus believers’ expenditure follows a just mean between extravagance and parsimony: the verse first negates both extremes and then explicitly affirms the middle path.
verses.68:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse prohibits shirk, unjust killing, and adultery. Although idolaters normally invoke lower gods rather than God, “calling upon another god with Allah” may mean that people inevitably call upon God through their fiṭrah; that invoking another god is to leave God for another while He exists; or that Arab polytheists invoked God at sea but their gods on land. The second explanation is the most plausible.

Believers do not kill a soul forbidden by Allah except for a just cause, such as retaliation (qiṣāṣ) or a legal penalty (ḥadd), and they do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse. “He who does this” (dhālika) encompasses all three acts—polytheism, unjust killing, and adultery—and athāman, synonymous with ithm, is the consequence of sin: the punishment sinners will face in the hereafter.
verses.69:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse elaborates the athām of the preceding verse: the offender’s punishment will be doubled on the Day of Resurrection, and disbelievers will remain in it forever, humiliated. Eternal punishment for polytheism is certain; the Qur’an also clearly affirms it for adultery and unjust killing, among Islam’s major sins, and likewise for usury.

Three explanations are possible. First, these sins may by their very nature call for eternal punishment independently of their doer’s belief or disbelief; this may be inferred from the apparent meaning of: Surely Allah does not forgive that anything should be associated with Him, and He forgives what is besides this to whom He wills (4:48, 4:116). Second, khulūd may mean a long stay, whether permanent or impermanent. Third, “he who does this” may refer to one who commits all three sins together, since the verse distinguishes believers, collectively free of these deeds, from disbelievers, collectively characterized by them.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan holds that the exception from meeting the requital of sin and abiding forever in punishment is conditional upon repentance, belief, and good deeds. Repentance is ceasing from sin, at its lowest degree through regret; without it one remains in one’s former practice. Righteous deeds make repentance firm, established, and sincere. Since īmān is a condition, the verse specifically concerns repentance from polytheism: it may concern those who committed all three preceding sins, or polytheists whether or not they committed the other two. Repentance from murder or adultery unaccompanied by polytheism is addressed by the next verse.

The fāʾ in “so these are they for whom Allah changes their evils into good” makes this transformation the consequence of their repentance, belief, and good deeds. Al-Mizan rejects, as departures from the apparent meaning without evidence, explanations that God merely records later obedience in place of earlier disobedience, changes an evil or good malakah, or substitutes rewards for the punishments due to sins. The apparent meaning is that their actual evils are changed into good.

A sayyiʾah is not the outward movement of an act, since the same movement may occur in both vice and virtue, such as sexual intercourse in adultery or lawful marriage, or taking property by usurpation or permission. Goodness and evil instead depend on conformity to God’s command. This leaves enduring traces and impressions in the soul, whereas the outward act passes away; these inner effects are what receive punishment in the hereafter, “on the day when the secrets are examined (86:9).” They also form a person’s actions: a wholly pure and virtuous essence cannot produce evil, while evil acts issue from an essence that is evil or mixed with evil.

When repentance, belief, and good deeds purify the essence so that it becomes free of defilement and wickedness, the traces inseparable from it become good as well. The transformation of evils into good is therefore through God’s forgiveness and mercy. Al-Mizan says the verse perhaps refers to something along these lines.
verses.71: Al-Mizan explains matāban as a verbal noun denoting tawbah, repentance or returning. The verse shows why the conversion of evils into good is not surprising: repentance is a special, goodly return to Allah, and God does what He wills. Unlike the preceding verse, which scarcely concerns sins not accompanied by polytheism, this verse applies to repentance from every sin, whether joined with polytheism or not.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, explains al-zūr as presenting falsehood so that it appears to be truth. It includes lying and false vanities such as singing (ghināʾ), profanity, and swearing. If zūr means lying, “do not witness falsehood” means that believers do not give false testimony; if it means such false vanities, it means they do not attend vain gatherings. The latter better accords with the remainder of the verse.

Laghw is any speech or action unworthy of attention because it has no rational aim, and thus includes all sins. When God’s special servants encounter people engaged in idleness and vanity, they pass by with dignity and aversion, keeping clear of entering their company, mixing with them, or joining their activity.
verses.73: Al-Mizan takes “falling down” (khurūr) here as a metaphor for fastening upon something or rushing toward it. When believers are reminded of their Lord’s communications and revelations, including the Qur’an’s wisdoms and fair exhortations, they do not receive them deaf and blind. Rather, they contemplate, understand, and accept them with insight; they believe their wisdom, heed their admonitions, see their path clearly, and follow the solid proof from their Lord.
verses.74:
Al-Mizan explains qurrata aʿyun as that which brings happiness and pleasure. The servants of God ask that their wives and offspring become the joy of their eyes by obeying God and refraining from disobedience. This is their sole concern, for they do not follow desires but care only for the truth.

Their request, “make us a leader to those who guard (against evil)” (lil-muttaqīn imāman), means that they ask to hasten toward good and strive for God’s mercy so that other muttaqūn follow them. The singular imām apparently indicates their wish to stand united in a single line ahead of the other Godwary. Other exegetical interpretations are that imām can be singular or plural; that it is the plural of āmm, making the sense, “Make us followers who head toward those who guard against evil”; and that an Ahl al-Bayt recitation reads, “Make for us a leader from those who guard against evil” (wa-ijʿal lanā min al-muttaqīna imāman).
verses.75:
Al-Mizan explains al-ghurfah as the upper part of a building and, here, an exalted rank in Paradise. The believers described above are granted these high ranks because of their patience, and angels receive them there with magnified greetings (taḥiyyatan) and salutations (salāman): a pleasant welcome and freedom from what is feared or avoided. Their abode and resting place are good, and they abide there.

The patience intended specifically includes patience in acts of obedience and patience in abstaining from disobedience, though neither is separable from patience in afflictions and tribulations.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains al-ghurfah as the upper part of a building and, here, an exalted rank in Paradise. The believers described above are granted these high ranks because of their patience, and angels receive them there with magnified greetings (taḥiyyatan) and salutations (salāman): a pleasant welcome and freedom from what is feared or avoided. Their abode and resting place are good, and they abide there.

The patience intended specifically includes patience in acts of obedience and patience in abstaining from disobedience, though neither is separable from patience in afflictions and tribulations.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan explains yaʿbaʾu through ʿibʾ, “weight” or “heaviness”: God’s not caring for them means that He sees no weight or worth in them. A different derivation has been proposed, yielding the sense that God would not spare or attend to them were it not for their calling.

The more plausible interpretation takes “your calling” (duʿāʾukum) as a verbal noun annexed to its object: it is God who calls them. The fāʾ in “for you have indeed rejected” makes their rejection the consequential explanation of why God has no regard for them. Their denial will bind closely to them until it brings everlasting punishment and inseparable wretchedness. Thus they have no value or station before their Lord—their existence and nonexistence are equal to Him—because they have denied His communications to the point that no good is hoped from them. If God calls them to truth and religion, it is only to complete the proof against them or that they may return from denial.

The alternative reading, according to which “your calling” means believers’ worship of God, does not accord with the consequential fāʾ. It also fails because annexing the verbal noun to its subject indicates an act already occurring, whereas the Meccan polytheists addressed by the verse did not worship or call upon God; the wording would instead have been “were it not for you to call Him” (law lā an tadʿūhu). The verse closes the sūrah by returning to its central theme: the polytheists’ objection to and rejection of God’s Messenger and the Qur’an revealed to him.
